title: Metric anchors, commitment pricing & usage psychology
content:
Context and objective:

This is a working GTM brief to align how Redwood positions token-based pricing alongside commitment (reserved) discounts and tier definitions. Goal is to give GTM (sales, CS, marketing) a coherent set of messages, simple math examples, and negotiation guardrails so teams sell consistently and protect unit economics.

Why this doc exists (problem statement):
- We need clear answers for: why token pricing vs seats or request-based; how to anchor value in product terms customers understand; and what discounting behavior we permit for committed spend.
- Current sales anecdotes show confusion: some prospects want per-seat pricing for internal devs, others ask for price-per-api-call. Sales sometimes over-discounts to close.

High-level positioning summary (one-liners):
- Token pricing: aligns cost to actual ML work and output quality — customers pay for what they generate and can optimize latency/quality tradeoffs without changing billing units.
- Commit discounts: reserved capacity reduces per-token unit cost and guarantees throughput; treat as a capacity/SLAs product (not a pure percent-off coupon).
- Tiers: simple three-tier structure (Starter, Scale, Enterprise) with clear usage and commitment thresholds, plus optional Dedicated/Private add-ons.

Principles that should guide all messaging:
1) Metric-first: anchor to a simple, measureable unit (tokens) that maps to engineering concerns (throughput, latency, model selection).
2) Predictability for growth: emphasize commit packages as insurance for cost and performance.
3) Preserve levers: discounts should reward committed revenue and predictable load — not unilateral negotiation for list price erosion.
4) Customer autonomy: tokens let customers trade latency/cost via model selection, batching, and cache rules without having to renegotiate pricing.

Why token pricing (talk track + supporting bullets for SDR/AE):
- Quick pitch: "We bill on tokens because that directly reflects the compute and model complexity powering your outputs — you only pay for what you use, and you can reduce cost by using caching, batching, or smaller models for non-critical flows."
- Supporting points to use in calls:
  - Tokens scale with model type + output length — easier to reason about generative workloads than requests or seats.
  - Enables hybrid workloads: high-throughput low-cost embedding jobs and low-volume high-quality generation can coexist under one contract.
  - Avoids seat inflation: seats encourage idle capacity and don’t reflect production token consumption.
  - Technical parity: tokens map to engineering metrics (tokens/sec, KV cache hits) so SRE/product teams can optimize without billing surprises.

Common rebuttals and scripts:
- Prospect: "We don’t like metered billing — we want predictable cost."
  - Reply: "We offer commit packages that convert usage to a predictable monthly effective rate and include autoscaling guarantees. You can also set hard caps and alerts to avoid surprises."
- Prospect: "We’d rather pay per-seat — that’s how most of our vendors price."
  - Reply: "Seats work for people-based collaboration tools; inference costs are driven by compute and tokens. With our token model you keep engineering incentives aligned — you can run more tests or internal tooling without negotiating more seats."

Tier and commitment structure (recommended):
- Starter (self-serve): pay-as-you-go token pricing, minimal commit options, developer perks (sandbox models, streaming), aimed at experimentation and PLG adoption.
- Scale (mid-market): monthly commitment band (e.g., $2k–$50k/month) with tiered unit discounts and basic SLA, tooling for cost monitoring and model pins.
- Enterprise: annual commitments > $600k ARR (example), deeper discounts, Dedicated capacity or Private deployment options, advanced SLA, compliance add-ons, white-glove onboarding.

Illustrative pricing math (simple examples for sales enablement) — keep numbers illustrative only:
- List token price: $0.0006 per token (example).
- Starter: PAYG $0.0006/token.
- Scale commit (example): $15k/month commit for 25M tokens/month effective rate = $0.0006 * 0.75 = $0.00045/token (25% effective discount) + guaranteed slot capacity during spikes.
- Enterprise commit: $500k/year for a blended $0.00028/token (roughly 55% effective discount) + Dedicated pool and escalation SLA.

Discounting guidance / guardrails (sales policy draft):
- Discounts should map to committed annual recurring revenue (ARR): 0% for PAYG, 15–30% for low commits (monthly), 30–55% for multi-year/large commits + Dedicated.
- Non-price concessions (faster SLAs, longer retention, free onboarding credits) preferred before steep price cuts.
- Never discount below a floor that breaks unit economics; each deal must route to Pricing Ops if requested discount > 40% without product concessions.
- Seat-like exceptions: allow hybrid offers (per-seat dev license + token bucket) only when seat pricing materially simplifies internal procurement — require a 12-month commit + minimum token bucket sized for estimated usage.

Competitive notes (short):
- Vendor A (request-based per-call): simple but obscures compute-heavy responses; customers complain about surprise bills when output length changes.
- Vendor B (seat + usage credits): straightforward for enterprise procurement but encourages overprovisioning and preserves vendor revenue per seat rather than per compute.
- Vendor C (time-based GPU minutes): good for infra teams, but poor fit for customers who value output-sized billing and model-switching flexibility.
- Our advantage: tokens + commits let product + infra teams optimize output quality vs cost with transparent unit economics and predictable reserved capacity.

Sales playbook snippets (short, copy-ready):
- Opening email line: "We price on tokens because it maps directly to the compute driving your app — that means you pay for what you generate and can reduce costs with simple optimizations like batching and caching."
- Discovery question: "What percent of your calls are short (<=64 tokens) vs long (>512 tokens)?" (helps recommend model/quantization and commit level)
- Close prompt for commit: "If we structure a 12-month commit at X/month, we can lock a Y% unit price and guarantee Z throughput for peak events — would that address your predictability concerns?"

Signals to measure post-sale (to protect economics):
- Tokens/month churn ratio — are customers increasing tokens as expected vs forecast?
- Model mix shift — heavier use of higher-capacity models should trigger an account review for capacity/price.
- Cache hit rate & average output length — product levers the customer can tune to reduce spend.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Finalize discount floors by segment (need finance input on acceptable unit margin per commit band).
- Build a sample calculator widget for AEs to show commit vs PAYG savings (UX to be spec’d with Product).
- Flesh out seat+bucket contract template for procurement-heavy customers (legal to draft).

Appendix: negotiation examples (realistic templates)
- Small ISV use-case: customer projects ~10M tokens/month. Recommend Scale band with 6-month commit; offer 20% discount + one month of onboarding credits. If they push for more, require a 12-month commit or product concessions (reduced retention).
- Enterprise retail chain: seasonal spikes (Black Friday). Offer Annual commit sized to baseline + burst override pricing at 1.5x committed unit rate; provide burst capacity SLA and committed pre-warmed pools.

Notes to self / signals for improvements:
- Integrate example math into internal pricing playbook and a one-click pricing calculator for AE kits.
- Add a short recording/badging for AEs on handling seat vs token pushback.
